answers.question_text: Q1. In the ShopStream lab, you sent the same order data to both Kinesis Data Streams and Firehose. The S3 outputs looked
answers.correct_answer: Data Streams (via Lambda) produced one JSON file per order with enriched fields (processed_at, priority_flag) organized as processed/year/month/day/. Firehose produced batched NDJSON files of raw untransformed orders organized as year/month/day/hour/. The difference is because Data Streams gives a programmable consumer (Lambda) for custom logic, while Firehose is a managed delivery pipe that buffers and flushes with zero transformation.

answers.question_text: Q2. A product manager says: "Firehose is simpler and cheaper — why would we ever use Kinesis Data Streams?" Give a speci
answers.correct_answer: Firehose cannot run custom logic on individual records. If ShopStream needs to flag high-value orders (over $500) in real time so the fulfillment team can prioritize them immediately, Firehose cannot do this. You need Kinesis Data Streams with a Lambda consumer that inspects each order, applies business logic, enriches the record, and writes the result within sub-second latency.

answers.question_text: Q3. In the lab, the Firehose buffer interval was set to 60 seconds. If you increased it to 300 seconds (5 minutes), how
answers.correct_answer: With a 300-second buffer, Firehose would accumulate more records before flushing, producing fewer but larger files. The trade-off is latency vs. efficiency: longer buffers mean data takes longer to appear in S3 (up to 5 minutes delay) but you get fewer larger files that are more efficient for downstream tools like Athena. Shorter buffers give fresher data but create the small file problem.

answers.question_text: Q4. When you connected Lambda to the Kinesis Data Stream, you configured a "starting position" of "Latest." What does th
answers.correct_answer: "Latest" means Lambda only processes records that arrive after the trigger is created, ignoring existing data. "Trim Horizon" means Lambda reads from the oldest available record in the stream (Kinesis retains data for 24 hours by default), processing all historical data. Trim Horizon is useful for reprocessing or catching up but can cause a burst of Lambda invocations.

answers.question_text: Q5. In the ShopStream lab, Lambda wrote one S3 object per order. If ShopStream scales to 1 million orders per day, why d
answers.correct_answer: One million individual S3 objects per day creates the "small file problem." S3 charges per request (PUT, GET, LIST) and query engines like Athena perform poorly with millions of small files. Alternative: batch records in Lambda — accumulate records and write one file per batch (e.g., every 1000 records or 30 seconds). This is essentially what Firehose does automatically.

answers.question_text: Q6. In the Week 7 lab, the December CSV had a "$" prefix on the price column (e.g., "$29.99"). Could you fix this by sim
answers.correct_answer: No. The Data Catalog stores metadata (column names, types, file locations) but does not change the actual data in S3. The string "$29.99" is physically in the CSV. Changing the catalog type to DOUBLE would cause Athena to fail with a parsing error or return NULL. You need ETL to strip the "$" and cast to a number — this is what the Glue Visual Editor SQL transform did with REGEXP_REPLACE. Metadata describes data; ETL transforms data.

answers.question_text: Q7. You ran a Glue Crawler on the orders data and it could have created three separate tables (one per month) instead of
answers.correct_answer: "Create a single schema for each S3 path" under Advanced Options / S3 Schema Grouping when configuring the Crawler. This merges all partitions into one table with a combined schema. Without it, the Crawler creates separate tables for each month, requiring UNION ALL queries instead of simple partitioned queries.

answers.question_text: Q8. In the Week 7 lab, November CSV added a "region" column that October didn't have, and December renamed "customer_id"
answers.correct_answer: Two problems: (1) The added region column: October rows return NULL for region — manageable, additive schema change. (2) The renamed customer_id to cust_id: CSV maps positionally so data lands correctly, but the Crawler sees two separate columns. October/November have customer_id populated but cust_id NULL; December has cust_id but customer_id NULL. Queries need COALESCE or ETL must standardize the column name.

answers.question_text: Q9. The Glue Visual Editor generated a PySpark script behind the scenes. Why might a data engineer choose to edit that g
answers.correct_answer: The Visual Editor has limits. A data engineer would switch to the script for: complex conditional logic, calling external APIs, custom error handling, multi-path pipelines, ML feature engineering, or transformations that can't be expressed in a single SQL block. The generated script is also version-controllable in Git for change tracking, code review, and rollback. Teams often start with the visual editor for prototyping and graduate to scripts.

answers.question_text: Q10. When you configured the Glue ETL job, you set the worker type to G.1X and requested 2 workers. Why does this matter
answers.correct_answer: Glue workers are compute resources that cost money per second. G.1X is the smallest worker type (4 vCPUs, 16 GB). For the lab's tiny dataset, 2 workers is enough. For 100x larger, increase workers (e.g., 10-20) so Spark can parallelize across machines, and possibly upgrade to G.2X (8 vCPUs, 32 GB) for more memory. Glue also offers auto-scaling for variable workloads.

answers.question_text: Q11. In the Week 6 lab, you ran the same query on the CSV table and the Parquet table. The query results were identical,
answers.correct_answer: Parquet is columnar — it stores column values together, so Athena reads only needed columns and skips the rest. CSV is row-based — reading one column requires scanning all columns. Parquet also uses compression (Snappy). This matters because Athena charges $5/TB scanned, so less data scanned = lower cost. At scale, this means thousands of dollars in annual savings.

answers.question_text: Q12. Query 3 in the basic lab (MIN, MAX, AVG on just the price column) showed the biggest gap between CSV and Parquet da
answers.correct_answer: Query 3 touched only ONE column (price) out of 10 total. Parquet reads only the price column (~1/10th of data). CSV must scan all 10 columns for every row. Queries 1 and 2 used 2-4 columns, so Parquet still won but the gap was smaller. The fewer columns needed relative to total, the bigger Parquet's advantage — especially powerful for analytics on wide tables.

answers.question_text: Q13. You built a three-tier folder structure: bronze, silver, and gold. Explain what each layer stores and why you would

Gold: pre-computed aggregations and KPIs for dashboards. Keep raw CSV in bronze because: (1) if conversion has a bug, re-run from original; (2) business requirements change, original is always available; (3) auditing and compliance; (4) easier to diagnose schema/quality issues.

Pay only per query ($5/TB scanned), and with Parquet on 50K rows each query costs fractions of a cent. RDS would require a 24/7 running instance costing money every hour even when idle. For a few queries per week, you'd pay for a server sitting idle 99%+ of the time. Athena queries S3 directly with no loading or ETL needed.

answers.question_text: Q15. Your bookstore uploads a new catalog CSV every month. If the new file has a column added in the middle of the exist
answers.correct_answer: CSV maps columns positionally — Athena reads the 1st value as column 1, 2nd as column 2, etc. A column inserted in the middle shifts every subsequent column, mapping wrong data to wrong columns (prices in rating column, etc.) with no error message. answers.question_text: Q11. In the Week 6 lab, you ran the same query on the CSV table and the Parquet table. The query results were identical,
answers.student_answer: Parquet files scan less data because it is columnar data, and each column is stored separately. answers.question_text: Q6. In the Week 7 lab, the December CSV had a "$" prefix on the price column (e.g., "$29.99"). Could you fix this by sim
answers.student_answer: No, this would not work because the data catalog only stores metadata; the actual string in the CSV file is in S3, and you would need an ETL to transform and take out the $ and actually change the value to a number.

answers.question_text: Q15. Your bookstore uploads a new catalog CSV every month. If the new file has a column added in the middle of the exist

answers.question_text: Q10. When you configured the Glue ETL job, you set the worker type to G.1X and requested 2 workers. Why does this matter
answers.correct_answer: Glue workers are compute resources that cost money per second. G.1X is the smallest worker type (4 vCPUs, 16 GB). For the lab's tiny dataset, 2 workers is enough. For 100x larger, increase workers (e.g., 10-20) so Spark can parallelize across machines, and possibly upgrade to G.2X (8 vCPUs, 32 GB) for more memory. Glue also offers auto-scaling for variable workloads.

answers.question_text: Q9. The Glue Visual Editor generated a PySpark script behind the scenes. Why might a data engineer choose to edit that g
answers.correct_answer: The Visual Editor has limits. A data engineer would switch to the script for: complex conditional logic, calling external APIs, custom error handling, multi-path pipelines, ML feature engineering, or transformations that can't be expressed in a single SQL block. answers.question_text: Q3. In the lab, the Firehose buffer interval was set to 60 seconds. If you increased it to 300 seconds (5 minutes), how
answers.correct_answer: With a 300-second buffer, Firehose would accumulate more records before flushing, producing fewer but larger files. The trade-off is latency vs. efficiency: longer buffers mean data takes longer to appear in S3 (up to 5 minutes delay) but you get fewer larger files that are more efficient for downstream tools like Athena. Shorter buffers give fresher data but create the small file problem.

answers.question_text: Q14. The analytics team runs ad-hoc queries on the 50,000-row book catalog a few times per week. Why is Athena a better
answers.correct_answer: Athena is serverless — no infrastructure to provision, manage, or pay for when idle. answers.question_text: Q11. In the Week 6 lab, you ran the same query on the CSV table and the Parquet table. The query results were identical,
answers.student_answer: Because Parquet is columnar, it only scan the necessary/targeted columns, and also compress the data to smaller size (compared to CSV), thus we will scan less data with Parquet. answers.question_text: Q6. In the Week 7 lab, the December CSV had a "$" prefix on the price column (e.g., "$29.99"). Could you fix this by sim
answers.student_answer: No. Because the Glue Data Catalog saves the metadata (data or information of the data), not modifies the original data.

You need ETL to strip the "$" and cast to a number — this is what the Glue Visual Editor SQL transform did with REGEXP_REPLACE. Metadata describes data; ETL transforms data.

answers.question_text: Q15. Your bookstore uploads a new catalog CSV every month. If the new file has a column added in the middle of the exist
answers.correct_answer: CSV maps columns positionally — Athena reads the 1st value as column 1, 2nd as column 2, etc. A column inserted in the middle shifts every subsequent column, mapping wrong data to wrong columns (prices in rating column, etc.) with no error message. answers.question_text: Q12. Query 3 in the basic lab (MIN, MAX, AVG on just the price column) showed the biggest gap between CSV and Parquet da
answers.correct_answer: Query 3 touched only ONE column (price) out of 10 total. Parquet reads only the price column (~1/10th of data). CSV must scan all 10 columns for every row. answers.question_text: Q13. You built a three-tier folder structure: bronze, silver, and gold. Explain what each layer stores and why you would
answers.student_answer:
Bronze layer stores raw files (CSV). 
Silver layer stores processed files (Parquet) ready to be scanned/queried efficiently.
Gold layer stores ready for business analysis or decision making.
We need to keep raw files in Bronze layer as our source of truth to accommodate future potential or strategic questions, and also for audit/compliance purpose (tracability).

Keep raw CSV in bronze because: (1) if conversion has a bug, re-run from original; (2) business requirements change, original is always available; (3) auditing and compliance; (4) easier to diagnose schema/quality issues.

answers.question_text: Q7. You ran a Glue Crawler on the orders data and it could have created three separate tables (one per month) instead of
answers.student_answer: If we want to create one unified table, we need to set the configuration of Create a Single Unified Schema.
answers.correct_answer: "Create a single schema for each S3 path" under Advanced Options / S3 Schema Grouping when configuring the Crawler. This merges all partitions into one table with a combined schema. Without it, the Crawler creates separate tables for each month, requiring UNION ALL queries instead of simple partitioned queries.

answers.question_text: Q1. In the ShopStream lab, you sent the same order data to both Kinesis Data Streams and Firehose. The S3 outputs looked
answers.student_answer: In the ShopStream lab, Kinesis Data Streams and Firehose produced different outputs because they serve different roles. By contrast, Firehose delivered incoming data in batches directly to S3 with minimal transformation, producing raw, batched files in the target bucket.

The difference is because Data Streams gives a programmable consumer (Lambda) for custom logic, while Firehose is a managed delivery pipe that buffers and flushes with zero transformation.

answers.question_text: Q5. In the ShopStream lab, Lambda wrote one S3 object per order. If ShopStream scales to 1 million orders per day, why d

answers.question_text: Q2. A product manager says: "Firehose is simpler and cheaper — why would we ever use Kinesis Data Streams?" Give a speci

If ShopStream needs to flag high-value orders (over $500) in real time so the fulfillment team can prioritize them immediately, Firehose cannot do this. You need Kinesis Data Streams with a Lambda consumer that inspects each order, applies business logic, enriches the record, and writes the result within sub-second latency.

Queries 1 and 2 used 2-4 columns, so Parquet still won but the gap was smaller. The fewer columns needed relative to total, the bigger Parquet's advantage — especially powerful for analytics on wide tables.

answers.question_text: Q13. You built a three-tier folder structure: bronze, silver, and gold. Explain what each layer stores and why you would
answers.correct_answer: Bronze: raw, as-received data in original format — never modified, source of truth. Silver: cleaned, typed, format-converted data (CSV to Parquet) for analytical queries. Gold: pre-computed aggregations and KPIs for dashboards. Keep raw CSV in bronze because: (1) if conversion has a bug, re-run from original; (2) business requirements change, original is always available; (3) auditing and compliance; (4) easier to diagnose schema/quality issues.

answers.question_text: Q7. You ran a Glue Crawler on the orders data and it could have created three separate tables (one per month) instead of
answers.correct_answer: "Create a single schema for each S3 path" under Advanced Options / S3 Schema Grouping when configuring the Crawler. This merges all partitions into one table with a combined schema. Without it, the Crawler creates separate tables for each month, requiring UNION ALL queries instead of simple partitioned queries.

answers.question_text: Q1. In the ShopStream lab, you sent the same order data to both Kinesis Data Streams and Firehose. The S3 outputs looked
answers.student_answer: data streams gives raw real-time data firehose buffers data and sends it to S3 in batches this is because data stream is for real-time processing while firehose is for simple delivery to storage.
answers.correct_answer: Data Streams (via Lambda) produced one JSON file per order with enriched fields (processed_at, priority_flag) organized as processed/year/month/day/. Firehose produced batched NDJSON files of raw untransformed orders organized as year/month/day/hour/. The difference is because Data Streams gives a programmable consumer (Lambda) for custom logic, while Firehose is a managed delivery pipe that buffers and flushes with zero transformation.

answers.question_text: Q5. In the ShopStream lab, Lambda wrote one S3 object per order. If ShopStream scales to 1 million orders per day, why d
answers.correct_answer: One million individual S3 objects per day creates the "small file problem." S3 charges per request (PUT, GET, LIST) and query engines like Athena perform poorly with millions of small files. Alternative: batch records in Lambda — accumulate records and write one file per batch (e.g., every 1000 records or 30 seconds). This is essentially what Firehose does automatically.

answers.question_text: Q2. A product manager says: "Firehose is simpler and cheaper — why would we ever use Kinesis Data Streams?" Give a speci
answers.correct_answer: Firehose cannot run custom logic on individual records. If ShopStream needs to flag high-value orders (over $500) in real time so the fulfillment team can prioritize them immediately, Firehose cannot do this. You need Kinesis Data Streams with a Lambda consumer that inspects each order, applies business logic, enriches the record, and writes the result within sub-second latency.

answers.question_text: Q8. In the Week 7 lab, November CSV added a "region" column that October didn't have, and December renamed "customer_id"
answers.correct_answer: Two problems: (1) The added region column: October rows return NULL for region — manageable, additive schema change. (2) The renamed customer_id to cust_id: CSV maps positionally so data lands correctly, but the Crawler sees two separate columns. October/November have customer_id populated but cust_id NULL; December has cust_id but customer_id NULL. Queries need COALESCE or ETL must standardize the column name.

answers.question_text: Q4. When you connected Lambda to the Kinesis Data Stream, you configured a "starting position" of "Latest." What does th
answers.correct_answer: "Latest" means Lambda only processes records that arrive after the trigger is created, ignoring existing data. "Trim Horizon" means Lambda reads from the oldest available record in the stream (Kinesis retains data for 24 hours by default), processing all historical data. Trim Horizon is useful for reprocessing or catching up but can cause a burst of Lambda invocations.

answers.question_text: Q10. When you configured the Glue ETL job, you set the worker type to G.1X and requested 2 workers. Why does this matter
answers.correct_answer: Glue workers are compute resources that cost money per second. G.1X is the smallest worker type (4 vCPUs, 16 GB). For the lab's tiny dataset, 2 workers is enough. For 100x larger, increase workers (e.g., 10-20) so Spark can parallelize across machines, and possibly upgrade to G.2X (8 vCPUs, 32 GB) for more memory. Glue also offers auto-scaling for variable workloads.

answers.question_text: Q9. The Glue Visual Editor generated a PySpark script behind the scenes. Why might a data engineer choose to edit that g
answers.student_answer: Editing the generated script directly can allow for more direct and precise edits that could lead to faster revisions than using the visual interface.
answers.correct_answer: The Visual Editor has limits. A data engineer would switch to the script for: complex conditional logic, calling external APIs, custom error handling, multi-path pipelines, ML feature engineering, or transformations that can't be expressed in a single SQL block. The generated script is also version-controllable in Git for change tracking, code review, and rollback. Teams often start with the visual editor for prototyping and graduate to scripts.

answers.question_text: Q3. In the lab, the Firehose buffer interval was set to 60 seconds. If you increased it to 300 seconds (5 minutes), how
answers.correct_answer: With a 300-second buffer, Firehose would accumulate more records before flushing, producing fewer but larger files. The trade-off is latency vs. efficiency: longer buffers mean data takes longer to appear in S3 (up to 5 minutes delay) but you get fewer larger files that are more efficient for downstream tools like Athena. Shorter buffers give fresher data but create the small file problem.

answers.question_text: Q14. The analytics team runs ad-hoc queries on the 50,000-row book catalog a few times per week. Why is Athena a better
answers.correct_answer: Athena is serverless — no infrastructure to provision, manage, or pay for when idle. Pay only per query ($5/TB scanned), and with Parquet on 50K rows each query costs fractions of a cent. RDS would require a 24/7 running instance costing money every hour even when idle. For a few queries per week, you'd pay for a server sitting idle 99%+ of the time. Athena queries S3 directly with no loading or ETL needed.

answers.question_text: Q11. In the Week 6 lab, you ran the same query on the CSV table and the Parquet table. The query results were identical,
answers.correct_answer: Parquet is columnar — it stores column values together, so Athena reads only needed columns and skips the rest. CSV is row-based — reading one column requires scanning all columns. Parquet also uses compression (Snappy). This matters because Athena charges $5/TB scanned, so less data scanned = lower cost. At scale, this means thousands of dollars in annual savings.

answers.question_text: Q6. In the Week 7 lab, the December CSV had a "$" prefix on the price column (e.g., "$29.99"). Could you fix this by sim
answers.student_answer: No you can't simply edit the column type to DOUBLE because the metadata would still be there.
answers.correct_answer: No. The Data Catalog stores metadata (column names, types, file locations) but does not change the actual data in S3. The string "$29.99" is physically in the CSV. Changing the catalog type to DOUBLE would cause Athena to fail with a parsing error or return NULL. You need ETL to strip the "$" and cast to a number — this is what the Glue Visual Editor SQL transform did with REGEXP_REPLACE. Metadata describes data; ETL transforms data.

answers.question_text: Q15. Your bookstore uploads a new catalog CSV every month. If the new file has a column added in the middle of the exist
answers.student_answer: Athena would have to scan additional data, leading to higher costs. This problem doesn't affect Parquet because Athena only queries relevant columns in Parquet, meaning the amount of data it scans does not change.
answers.correct_answer: CSV maps columns positionally — Athena reads the 1st value as column 1, 2nd as column 2, etc. A column inserted in the middle shifts every subsequent column, mapping wrong data to wrong columns (prices in rating column, etc.) with no error message. Parquet stores column names inside the file and maps by name, not position, so reordering/adding columns doesn't cause misalignment. Parquet is inherently safer for schema evolution.
